BEGINNER1. What is Async/Await?

async/await is syntax built on top of Promises that lets asynchronous code READ like synchronous code — no .then() chains needed.

Real-world analogy: An async function is a chef's recipe that may involve waiting. await is a step like "wait for the pasta to boil" — the chef pauses just THIS recipe, but the rest of the kitchen (the event loop) keeps running. 
// Promise-based (.then chain)
function loadUser() {
    return fetch("/api/user")
        .then(res => res.json())
        .then(user => console.log(user));
}

// Same logic with async/await — reads top to bottom
async function loadUser2() {
    const res = await fetch("/api/user");
    const user = await res.json();
    console.log(user);
}

BEGINNER2. async Functions Always Return a Promise

Marking a function async guarantees it returns a Promise — even if the code inside looks like it's returning a plain value.

async function getNumber() {
    return 42; // automatically wrapped: Promise.resolve(42)
}

console.log(getNumber());          // Promise { 42 }  — NOT 42 directly!
getNumber().then(n => console.log(n)); // 42 — must unwrap with .then() or await

// Throwing inside an async function REJECTS the returned promise
async function fail() {
    throw new Error("boom");
}
fail().catch(e => console.log(e.message)); // "boom"
⚠️ Common Pitfall: Calling an async function does NOT block or wait — it immediately returns a pending Promise. You must await it (inside another async function) or use .then() to get the actual resolved value.

BEGINNER3. The await Keyword

await pauses execution of the CURRENT async function until the Promise to its right settles, then "unwraps" it into the resolved value — no .then() callback needed.

function delay(ms, value) {
    return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve(value), ms));
}

async function run() {
    console.log("before");
    const result = await delay(1000, "done!");
    console.log(result); // "done!" — printed after the 1-second pause
    console.log("after");
}
run();
// Output order: "before" immediately, then (after 1s) "done!" then "after"
💡 Tip: await only pauses the ASYNC FUNCTION it's inside — it does NOT block the rest of the program. Other code (other functions, UI events, timers) keeps running normally while an async function is paused at an await.

await can only be used directly inside a function marked async (with one modern exception — see Section 8).

// function loadData() {
//     const data = await fetch(url); // ❌ SyntaxError — not inside an async function
// }

async function loadData() {
    const data = await fetch(url); // ✅ works
}

INTERMEDIATE4. Error Handling with try/catch/finally

A rejected await throws — exactly like a synchronous throw — so wrap it in a regular try/catch block.

async function loadUser(id) {
    try {
        const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        const user = await res.json();
        return user;
    } catch (err) {
        console.error("Failed to load user:", err.message);
        return null; // graceful fallback
    } finally {
        hideSpinner(); // always runs, success or failure
    }
}

function hideSpinner() { console.log("spinner hidden"); }
Promise-chain error handling: 
function loadUser(id) {
    return fetch(`/api/users/${id}`)
        .then(res => res.json())
        .catch(err => {
            console.error(err);
            return null;
        });
}
async/await error handling: 
async function loadUser(id) {
    try {
        const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
        return await res.json();
    } catch (err) {
        console.error(err);
        return null;
    }
}

INTERMEDIATE5. Sequential vs Parallel Execution

Awaiting one thing after another RUNS them sequentially — each waits for the previous one to finish. If the operations are independent, this wastes time. Use Promise.all() to run them in parallel.

// ❌ Sequential — total time = timeA + timeB (e.g. 2s + 2s = 4s)
async function loadSequential() {
    const user = await fetchUser();   // waits ~2s
    const posts = await fetchPosts(); // THEN waits another ~2s
    return { user, posts };
}

// ✅ Parallel — total time = max(timeA, timeB) (e.g. max(2s, 2s) = 2s)
async function loadParallel() {
    const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([
        fetchUser(),
        fetchPosts()
    ]);
    return { user, posts };
}
⚠️ When You SHOULD Be Sequential: If the second call depends on the result of the first (e.g. you need the user's ID before fetching their posts), sequential awaits are correct and necessary — parallelizing would be impossible or wrong. 
// Correct sequential use — posts genuinely depend on user.id
async function loadUserAndPosts() {
    const user = await fetchUser();          // must finish first
    const posts = await fetchPosts(user.id); // needs user.id from above
    return { user, posts };
}

ADVANCED6. Awaiting Non-Promises

await works fine on a value that ISN'T a Promise — it just returns that value immediately (wrapped as if it were Promise.resolve(value)), no error.

async function test() {
    const x = await 42;       // not a promise — returns 42 directly
    console.log(x);           // 42

    const y = await "hello";  // same idea
    console.log(y);           // "hello"

    const z = await Promise.resolve(99); // works the same as a real promise
    console.log(z);           // 99
}
test();

ADVANCED7. Async/Await Inside Loops

forEach() does NOT wait for async callbacks — it fires them all and moves on immediately. Use for...of for sequential async work, or Promise.all + map for parallel async work.

const ids = [1, 2, 3];

// ❌ WRONG — forEach ignores the promises returned by its async callback
async function processAllWrong() {
    ids.forEach(async (id) => {
        await process(id);
    });
    console.log("Done"); // logs almost IMMEDIATELY, before any processing finishes!
}

// ✅ CORRECT — for...of properly awaits each iteration, one at a time
async function processSequential() {
    for (const id of ids) {
        await process(id);
    }
    console.log("Done"); // logs only after ALL are processed, in order
}

// ✅ CORRECT — Promise.all + map for concurrent processing
async function processParallel() {
    await Promise.all(ids.map(id => process(id)));
    console.log("Done"); // logs after all finish, but they ran concurrently
}

function process(id) {
    return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => { console.log("processed", id); resolve(); }, 100));
}

ADVANCED8. Top-Level Await

Modern ES modules (files loaded with type="module", or .mjs) allow await directly at the top level, OUTSIDE any async function.

// Inside an ES module (e.g. <script type="module"> or a .mjs file):
const response = await fetch("/api/config");
const config = await response.json();
console.log(config); // works without wrapping in an async function!

// This is NOT allowed in regular (non-module) scripts or CommonJS files —
// you'd need to wrap it in an async IIFE there instead:
(async () => {
    const response = await fetch("/api/config");
    console.log(await response.json());
})();

ADVANCED9. Common Pitfalls

1. Forgetting await Entirely

async function getData() {
    return fetchData();
}

async function run() {
    const data = getData(); // ❌ forgot await — data is a Promise, not the resolved value!
    console.log(data);      // Promise {  }

    const data2 = await getData(); // ✅ correct
    console.log(data2);            // actual resolved value
}

2. Unnecessary Sequential Awaits

// ❌ Slower than necessary — these don't depend on each other
async function loadDashboard() {
    const stats = await fetchStats();
    const notifications = await fetchNotifications();
    return { stats, notifications };
}

// ✅ Run independent calls in parallel
async function loadDashboardFast() {
    const [stats, notifications] = await Promise.all([
        fetchStats(),
        fetchNotifications()
    ]);
    return { stats, notifications };
}

3. Missing try/catch Around await

// ❌ An unhandled rejection crashes/rejects silently up the call stack
async function loadUser() {
    const res = await fetch("/api/user"); // if this rejects, no catch here
    return res.json();
}

// ✅ Always wrap risky awaits
async function loadUserSafe() {
    try {
        const res = await fetch("/api/user");
        return await res.json();
    } catch (err) {
        console.error(err);
        return null;
    }
}

4. Using forEach for Async Work

// ❌ Does not wait — see Section 7 for the full explanation
items.forEach(async (item) => await save(item));

// ✅ Use for...of or Promise.all + map instead
for (const item of items) { await save(item); }

INTERMEDIATE10. Best Practices

1. Always Wrap await in try/catch

// ✅ Predictable failure handling
async function safeFetch(url) {
    try {
        const res = await fetch(url);
        return await res.json();
    } catch (err) {
        return { error: err.message };
    }
}

2. Use Promise.all for Independent Operations

// ✅ Faster, still readable
const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB(), fetchC()]);

3. Use for...of, Not forEach, for Sequential Async Work

// ✅ Correctly waits for each iteration
for (const id of ids) {
    await processOne(id);
}

4. Don't Mix .then() and await Unnecessarily

// ✅ Pick one style per function for consistency
async function load() {
    const data = await fetchData();
    return data;
}

// ❌ Mixing styles adds confusion
async function loadMixed() {
    return fetchData().then(data => data);
}

5. Name Async Functions Clearly

// ✅ The name signals it returns a promise / does async work
async function fetchUserProfile(id) { /* ... */ }

📋 Quick Reference Summary

Concept Key Points
async function Always returns a Promise, even when returning a plain value.
await Pauses the async function (not the whole program) until the Promise settles.
Error handling Rejected awaits throw — use standard try/catch/finally.
Sequential vs parallel Independent awaits should use Promise.all, not one after another.
Loops forEach ignores async callbacks — use for...of or Promise.all + map.
Top-level await Allowed directly in ES modules; needs an async IIFE elsewhere.

🎓 Learning Path

Beginner: Master sections 1, 2, 3

Intermediate: Understand sections 4, 5, 10

Advanced: Deep dive into sections 6, 7, 8, 9
